On August 24, Oriel Bachar filed a deposition notice (Dkt. 77) in Case No. 26-11217 before Judge Walrath. The filing arrives one day before Papaya's objection deadline to Skillz's Motion to Compel Production of Documents and Certain Deposition Witnesses (Dkt. 73, objections due August 26), and three days before the virtual discovery hearing (Dkt. 76, August 28, 10:00 a.m. ET, Courtroom 4). The notice is substantive in classification — it is the foreign representative's own deposition notice, filed in direct response to the discovery dispute Skillz forced to a head via Dkt. 73 — but its significance is bounded: it reflects Papaya's willingness to put a witness forward, which potentially narrows the factual dispute before the court on Thursday, but it does not resolve whether Skillz's broader document production demands will be satisfied.

The strategic read is that Papaya filed Dkt. 77 ahead of its written objection to blunt at least the deposition-witness prong of Skillz's motion to compel. Skillz's Dkt. 73 attacked on two fronts — document production deficiencies and the availability of deposition witnesses — and Papaya's deposition notice, filed before the objection deadline, signals a concession on the witness availability issue while leaving the document production fight open. If Papaya's August 26 objection confirms that posture, the August 28 hearing before Judge Walrath may sharpen to a narrower dispute over the sufficiency of document production rather than the full scope of Dkt. 73. That would be a partial win for Skillz — it secures the deposition — but would leave unresolved how much of the underlying documentary record Skillz can build before the recognition hearing.

For recovery analysis, nothing has shifted structurally. 
Judge Cote ordered Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement, as well as approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and legal costs
 — that judgment remains stayed as to U.S. assets under Judge Walrath's temporary injunction. 
Papaya applied to the Tel Aviv District Court for a temporary stay, under which the company's available cash and current profits would be transferred to a designated fund held by an authorized representative on behalf of the court, intended to safeguard creditors' rights if Papaya's appeal is ultimately rejected.
 The adequacy of that fund — and Skillz's ability to contest recognition — still turns on how much of a factual record Skillz can assemble. Dkt. 77 represents one data point in that build. The next two hard deadlines are Papaya's written objection to Dkt. 73 on August 26 and the virtual discovery hearing before Judge Walrath on August 28, where the court will rule on the scope and timing of any compelled production.

Today, Skillz Platform Inc. filed a Motion to Compel Production of Documents and Certain Deposition Witnesses (Dkt. 73) and a companion Motion to Shorten Notice with respect to that motion (Dkt. 74), both by counsel Michael Neiburg — the most significant escalation on this docket since the deposition notices filed August 11. The motion to compel (Dkt. 73) attaches seven exhibits (Exhibits A through G), signaling a detailed factual record of alleged deficiencies in Papaya's discovery responses: the volume of exhibits is consistent with a party documenting repeated meet-and-confer attempts and specific document categories or witness designations in dispute. The motion to shorten notice (Dkt. 74) is the operative tell: Skillz is not content to wait out a standard notice period and is pressing Judge Walrath to schedule hearing on the underlying motion on an expedited basis, which carries an implicit argument that delay causes prejudice — almost certainly a prejudice tied to an upcoming recognition hearing date. Together, Dkts. 73 and 74 are substantive and important: a motion to compel is an adversarial discovery filing that, in a Chapter 15 context, directly bears on the evidentiary record Skillz needs to contest recognition, and the request for shortened notice signals that Skillz believes a deadline is close enough to make ordinary scheduling inadequate.

The rescheduled hearing notice at Dkt. 71 (filed August 19) is the procedural counterpart worth flagging here — not for its own weight, but because a hearing rescheduling, read alongside Skillz's same-day push to shorten notice on a new motion, suggests that the original hearing calendar has shifted and that Skillz is now racing to complete discovery before a revised hearing date. Dkt. 70, the Order entered August 18 on the heels of Papaya's Certification of Counsel (Dkt. 69), may have set or reset that date; its full text remains unconfirmed in any publicly accessible source and requires PACER review to close that gap. If Dkt. 70 shortened the recognition hearing timeline, that would explain the compressed posture Skillz is projecting today. The deposition notices Skillz filed August 11 (Dkts. 61–62) established that both sides were building records for a contested hearing; Dkts. 73 and 74 confirm that Skillz believes Papaya's production to date is materially incomplete — and that it intends to litigate that deficiency before the recognition hearing rather than absorb the gap.

For creditors and recovery analysis, the significance is structural: Skillz/Firy's ability to contest recognition — and ultimately to resume collection against the approximately $719 million disgorgement judgment plus approximately $10.1 million in fees entered by Judge Cote — depends on the evidentiary record it builds now. 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction immediately stayed collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets, preserving the status quo pending the recognition hearing.
 A motion to compel, if granted, accelerates that evidentiary build and strengthens Skillz's ability to argue at the recognition hearing that the Israeli proceeding does not meet the requirements for recognition — or that the terms of any recognized proceeding should not include continuation of the stay. Papaya's posture — what it has withheld or declined to produce — will become clearer only when the full motion and exhibits are reviewed. The next concrete milestone is Judge Walrath's ruling on the motion to shorten notice (Dkt. 74), which will set the hearing date on the motion to compel (Dkt. 73) and, by extension, define the evidentiary cutoff before the recognition hearing itself. Dkt. 72 (Certificate of Service, August 19) is procedural and routine.

Delaware), one day after Papaya Gaming's counsel filed the Certification of Counsel at Dkt. 69. The turnaround confirms that the matter presented by the certification was either fully consensual or sufficiently uncontested that Judge Walrath was prepared to act without a hearing. Under standard Delaware bankruptcy practice, a COC certifies to the court that any objection period has run without opposition — or that all interested parties have agreed on the proposed order's form — and asks the judge to enter the order off the docket. The one-business-day response here is at the short end of typical but not unusual for an agreed-upon or unopposed matter.

The substance of Dkt. 70 remains unverified in the public record accessed for this briefing: neither the docket entry text nor any secondary source available as of today discloses what the order addresses. The two live substantive threads on this docket are (1) the scheduling of the recognition hearing on Papaya's Chapter 15 petition and (2) the scope and duration of Judge Walrath's temporary injunction staying collection and enforcement against Papaya's U.S. assets — the relief that continues to block Firy Inc. (formerly Skillz) from enforcing Judge Cote's judgment of approximately $719 million in disgorgement plus approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and costs. 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction immediately stayed collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets, preserving the status quo pending a hearing on Papaya's petition for formal recognition under Chapter 15.
 If Dkt. 70 sets or confirms that recognition hearing date, it becomes the governing milestone for the stay's duration and for Skillz/Firy's collection timeline; if it is administrative — a stipulated schedule extension, a sealing order, or similar — it carries no independent weight on recovery. Confirmation of the order's content requires the full text of Dkt. 70, which should be accessible through PACER.

The deposition notices filed August 11 (Dkts. 61–62) remain the operative evidentiary posture signal: both sides are building records for a contested recognition hearing, not standing down. The next concrete milestone is confirmation of the recognition hearing date — either disclosed by Dkt. 70 itself or by a subsequent scheduling order. On August 17, Papaya Gaming's counsel filed a Certification of Counsel (Dkt. 69) in Case No. 26-11217 before Judge Mary F. Walrath, U.S. Bankruptcy Court, D. Delaware. A Certification of Counsel is the standard Delaware bankruptcy mechanism by which a party certifies that no objection has been received — or that all parties have agreed on form — and submits a proposed order directly to the judge for entry without a hearing. The underlying subject matter of the proposed order is not disclosed on the face of the docket entry, and the full text of Dkt. 69 is not available in the public record accessed for this briefing; the content and significance of the order it seeks remain unverified until either the document itself or the court's response order appears on the docket. What is clear is that a proposed order is now sitting with Judge Walrath awaiting entry, and the matter was sufficiently uncontested — or resolved among the parties — to proceed by certification rather than noticed motion. If the proposed order relates to scheduling the recognition hearing or to the scope of the temporary injunction (the two live substantive threads on this docket), it would carry material consequence for Skillz/Firy's collection timeline; if it is administrative in nature, it carries none. Confirmation requires the court's responsive order, which should appear on the docket within days of the certification.

The active substantive posture is otherwise unchanged: 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets, preserving the status quo pending a hearing on Papaya's petition for formal recognition under Chapter 15
, and 
that relief was granted despite strong opposition from Skillz, now operating as Firy Inc.
 The deposition notices filed August 11 (Dkts. 61–62) remain the clearest signal that both sides are building evidentiary records for the recognition hearing rather than standing down. 
Judge Cote's underlying judgment requires Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement, as well as approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and legal costs
 — the full amount blocked from collection while the temporary injunction holds. For Skillz/Firy, a denial of recognition remains the path to enforcement; 
if the Delaware bankruptcy court approves the petition, Skillz would be blocked from collecting on the $719 million judgment while Papaya's appeal plays out.


The next concrete milestone is the court's entry of whatever order Dkt. 69 proposes — likely within the next two to five business days, absent judicial hold. If that order sets or confirms the recognition hearing date, it becomes the governing milestone for the stay's duration and creditor recovery timing.

items.body_md:
On August 11, Firy filed two additional deposition notices (Dkts. 61–62) and two affidavits (Dkts. 66–67) in Case No. 26-11217 before Judge Walrath, both filings bearing on the contested Chapter 15 recognition proceeding. The deposition notices extend Firy's witness program beyond the three already noticed August 8 — Oriel Bachar, Pinni Yaniv, and James Kong (Dkts. 53–55) — adding two further deponents whose identities are not specified in the docket entry text. That expansion signals Firy is pressing a broad factual record ahead of the recognition hearing, consistent with the strategic posture of a creditor seeking to challenge the foreign proceeding's eligibility or the scope of the temporary injunction Judge Walrath granted August 9.

The two affidavits (Dkts. 66–67) are the more consequential August 11 filings. In a contested Chapter 15 recognition proceeding, sworn affidavits typically function as evidentiary support for a party's position on recognition eligibility, the debtor's center-of-main-interests, or the terms under which a temporary injunction should be continued or dissolved. The docket record does not specify which party submitted them or what propositions they address; that detail will control how they bear on Firy's recovery posture. If they are Papaya-side submissions, they likely shore up the COMI analysis or the Israeli fund structure. If Firy-side, they are likely directed at contesting one of those same points. Until the documents themselves are reviewed, the filing cannot be assigned a directional weight — but their timing, three affidavits-and-depositions days into a contested proceeding with no recognition hearing date yet set, confirms both sides are building a litigation record at pace.

Three further pro hac vice motions were filed August 10 (Dkts. 58–60), continuing the counsel-buildout on the Firy side that the Latham & Watkins admissions (Dkts. 56–57, approving Ardeljan and Quartarolo) completed the same day. Dkts. 63–65, three additional pro hac vice motions filed August 11, deepen that roster further. No recognition hearing date appears on the docket as of this briefing; that date, once set, will be the controlling deadline against which both sides' deposition and affidavit schedules are paced.

items.body_md:
On August 9, Judge Mary F. Walrath of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware granted Papaya Gaming's motion for a temporary injunction. 
The order immediately stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets and preserves the status quo pending a hearing on Papaya's petition for formal recognition under Chapter 15.
 
The relief was granted over strong opposition from Firy Inc. (formerly Skillz), whose demands Judge Walrath rejected.
 The injunction is the central near-term protection Papaya sought when it filed: without it, Firy could have moved to attach U.S. assets before recognition is adjudicated, potentially disrupting the Israeli-supervised fund structure on which any eventual recovery to claimants depends.


Judge Cote's underlying July 27 order required Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement plus approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and costs.
 The temporary injunction does not disturb that judgment or Papaya's pending appeal of it; it only freezes enforcement in the U.S. pending the Chapter 15 recognition hearing. For Firy as the sole material creditor, the practical consequence is that U.S.-side collection — including any post-judgment asset discovery or attachment — is halted for now. 
Under the terms Papaya presented to the Israeli court, it will transfer available cash into a designated fund overseen by a court-appointed official, with the fund expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 and additional tens of millions annually, constituting the potential source for claim settlement if the U.S. ruling becomes enforceable in Israel.
 The gap between that fund and the $729 million total exposure remains the defining recovery variable; the recognition hearing will be the next moment at which that gap is formally tested.

Dkts. 56 through 60 — pro hac vice orders for Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo of Latham & Watkins (on Skillz/Firy's behalf) and three further pro hac vice motions filed August 10 — confirm that Firy is assembling a full Latham team alongside its existing Weil Gotshal roster. That concentration of outside counsel on Firy's side signals active preparation for the recognition hearing, consistent with the deposition notices Skillz filed August 8 targeting Oriel Bachar, Pinni Yaniv, and James Kong (Dkts. 53–55). The next concrete milestone is the recognition hearing before Judge Walrath, at which she will determine whether to grant Chapter 15 recognition to the Israeli proceeding and whether the temporary injunction should be extended, modified, or dissolved — no date for that hearing is reflected on the docket as of this briefing.

items.body_md:
The principal development since Friday's briefing is substantive: 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction now provides Papaya with legal protection in the United States while the Chapter 15 proceedings move forward.
 
Judge Walrath rejected Skillz's demands and granted Papaya's request.
 The injunction stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets pending the recognition hearing, which Dkt. 40/41 has already scheduled for September 3, 2026. This is meaningful movement: what the § 1519 provisional stay had established provisionally is now reinforced by a formal injunctive order entered before recognition — a stronger posture for Papaya during the appeal window, and a corresponding constraint on Firy/Skillz's near-term enforcement options in the United States.

That posture is now being tested in discovery. Dkts. 52–55, all filed August 8 by Skillz counsel Sean Beach, are three deposition notices — targeting Oriel Bachar (Papaya's co-founder and CEO), Pinni Yaniv, and James Kong — accompanied by a notice of service. 
Papaya is represented in the Israeli proceeding by attorney Pini Yaniv, a partner in the litigation department at Meitar Law Offices.
 Skillz is plainly using the pre-recognition window to build a factual record, most likely to contest whether the Israeli proceeding qualifies as a foreign main proceeding under 11 U.S.C. § 1517, to challenge the adequacy of the supervised payment arrangement as protection for creditors, or both. The three witnesses span the petitioner herself, Israeli legal counsel, and a third individual whose role is not confirmed in available materials. Dkts. 50 and 51 — pro hac vice motions for Latham & Watkins' Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo, filed August 7 — have now expanded Skillz's Delaware counsel roster to five Latham practitioners, alongside local counsel Beach. That depth of Latham coverage, paired with aggressive pre-hearing discovery, signals that Skillz intends to contest recognition on the merits rather than simply register objections.

From a recovery standpoint, the temporary injunction forecloses the immediate collection path Skillz would need to reach U.S. assets before September 3. The structural ceiling, however, is unchanged: 
Papaya applied to the Tel Aviv District Court for a temporary stay of proceedings, and under the proposed arrangement, the company's available cash and current profits would be transferred to a designated fund held by an authorized representative on behalf of the court — an arrangement intended to safeguard creditors' rights if Papaya's appeal is ultimately rejected.
 That fund was estimated at approximately $100 million during 2026, against a judgment face value of 
approximately $719 million in disgorgement, as well as approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and legal costs.
 The deposition schedule adds procedural complexity before the recognition hearing but does not, by itself, alter that gap. Objections to recognition are due August 27, 2026; the recognition hearing is set for September 3, 2026 at 9:30 AM (virtual).

The 72-hour window produced no substantive docket movement. Dkts. 50 and 51, both filed August 7, are pro hac vice admission motions, continuing the run of practitioner-entry filings that began August 6 (Dkts. 43–49). That brings the two-day total to nine entries — one appearance notice, five pro hac vice motions, and three corresponding admission orders — all procedural, none dispositive. The recognition hearing date set by Dkt. 40 remains the operative next milestone; the date itself is not confirmed in the docket ground truth available and should be verified against PACER directly. The volume of new appearances continues to expand the counsel roster well beyond the debtor and primary judgment creditor, consistent with additional interested parties establishing standing before recognition is decided, but the identities of the newly admitted practitioners are not confirmed in available materials.

One parallel development in the New York proceeding warrants attention as background context. 
The Southern District of New York has a separate opinion addressing Firy's request for injunctive relief that remains forthcoming
 — this was flagged in Firy's July 28 press release but has not yet issued. If Judge Cote enters a broad injunction against Papaya's business practices before the Delaware recognition hearing resolves, the interaction between that order and the § 1519 provisional stay will become a live question: injunctive relief directed at conduct rather than collection would not be automatically stayed by § 1519 or § 1520 in the same way a money judgment enforcement action would be, and Papaya would likely need to seek additional relief or argue the scope of the stay covers it. That is a contingent scenario, not a current one, but the pendency of the injunction opinion means it could materialize on short notice.

The structural recovery constraint remains unchanged: the § 1519 provisional stay is operative, the recognition hearing has been scheduled but not yet heard, and the Israeli-court-supervised fund — expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 — represents the practical ceiling on near-term recovery regardless of what happens in Delaware. The gap between that figure and the $719 million judgment face value (plus approximately $10 million in awarded attorney's fees, per __[Firy Inc. / BusinessWire press release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260728653231/en/Federal-Court-Orders-Papaya-Gaming-to-Pay-$719-Million-to-Skillz-Platform-Inc.-a-FIRY-NYSE-FIRY-Company-Disgorging-Its-Unjust-Profits-From-False-Advertising)__) is not closed by anything that moved this week. items.body_md:
The two most consequential filings of the week both landed on August 5. Judge Mary F. Walrath signed Dkt. 39, the Order Granting Provisional Relief Pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 1519 — putting a U.S. statutory stay in place pending the recognition hearing — and simultaneously entered Dkt. 40, the Order Scheduling the Hearing on Recognition of the Chapter 15 Petition and specifying the form and manner of notice. Those two orders together convert what was, through Tuesday, a petition supported only by the Tel Aviv District Court's August 2 domestic stay into a proceeding with active U.S. federal protection. 
If the Delaware court grants full recognition, Firy Inc. (formerly Skillz) would be blocked from collecting on the $719 million judgment while Papaya's appeal runs its course.
 The § 1519 provisional order holds that position in the interim. Dkt. 41, filed the same day, is the notice of hearing distributed to parties; Dkt. 42, filed August 5, is the certificate of service confirming that distribution went out.

Yesterday, August 6, the docket absorbed six more practitioner-entry filings — Dkts. 43 through 49 — consisting of one appearance notice and three pro hac vice motions (Dkts. 44–46) paired with three corresponding admission orders (Dkts. 47–49). Four pro hac vice admissions were already entered by order on August 4 (covering Coleman, Raynal, Carpenito, and Davidson per Dkts. 29–32), so the roster of admitted counsel is now materially larger. That volume of new appearances at this early stage suggests parties beyond the debtor and the primary judgment creditor are positioning themselves in the proceeding — the identities of the newly appearing counsel are not confirmed in the materials available, but the pattern is consistent with additional creditors or interested parties establishing standing ahead of the recognition hearing. The recognition hearing date itself was set by Dkt. 40 but is not confirmed in the current docket ground truth; 
the next key threshold question is whether the U.S. Bankruptcy Court will grant Chapter 15 recognition.


For Firy's recovery posture, the operative tension remains unchanged in structure but has now sharpened in timing: provisional § 1519 relief is live, which means collection is stayed, but the recognition order — the mechanism that makes that stay durable — has not yet issued. 
Under the terms presented to the Israeli court, Papaya will transfer available cash balances into a designated fund overseen by a court-appointed official, with that fund expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 as a potential source for settling claims should the U.S. ruling become enforceable in Israel.
 
The $719 million disgorgement figure was entered in lieu of the $420 million in actual damages awarded by the jury in April 2026, as Firy is entitled to recover once for its injury.
 The gap between the fund's projected 2026 ceiling and the judgment face value is the central recovery constraint, and the pace at which that fund is populated — and by whom it is overseen — will deserve close attention as the Israeli proceeding develops in parallel. The next concrete milestone in Delaware is the recognition hearing scheduled by Dkt. 40; that date governs when Judge Walrath can enter the order that would make the automatic-stay effect of § 1520 operative against Firy's collection efforts on a permanent rather than provisional basis.
